alignment.note: The Syriac collapses the conjunction and verb into a single prefixed form ܘܐܡܪ ('and-he-said'), whereas Greek καὶ εἶπεν and Latin Et dixit keep the conjunction and verb as discrete tokens; this is a purely orthographic-morphological feature of Syriac prefix conjugation, not a semantic divergence.

Greek uses an aorist passive participle πορευθέντες ('having gone') and Latin a present participle Euntes ('going'), both subordinating the action to the main imperative; Syriac ܙܠܘ is a bare imperative ('go!'), turning the participial circumstance into a coordinate command — a construction-level difference common in Semitic rendering of Greek participial chains.
εἰς τὸν κόσμον / ܠܥܠܡܐ / in mundum: the Syriac prefix ܠ subsumes the preposition and article into the noun, matching the Greek prepositional phrase and Latin accusative of motion.

Greek imperative κηρύξατε and Latin imperative prædicate stand asyndetically after the participle, whereas Syriac ܘܐܟܪܙܘ adds the coordinating ܘ ('and proclaim'), reflecting the imperative-coordination noted above; the verbal root k-r-z is itself a loan reflecting the same Hellenistic preaching vocabulary.

τὸ εὐαγγέλιον / ܣܒܪܬܝ / Evangelium: while the Latin retains the Greek loanword, the Syriac here employs the native Aramaic noun ('good tidings'), a lexical substitution from a Semitic root rather than the transliterated Greek term used elsewhere in the verse.

πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει / ܒܟܠܗ ܒܪܝܬܐ / omni creaturæ: all three render 'to/in all creation'; the Syriac prefixes ܒ ('in/to') and incorporates the article into ܟܠܗ, while the noun ܒܪܝܬܐ derives from the root b-r-y ('to create'), semantically equivalent to κτίσις and creatura.
